messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sofia was thirty-nine years old, a staff sergeant in the Army, and had spent fourteen years believing she could handle anything. That belief ended during the hurricane. She had been stationed at a coastal base when the storm surge came through, and for six hours she was pinned in a collapsed supply building with water rising to her chest, debris battering the metal walls, and the sound of the roof tearing away in sheets. She remembered the way the air pressure changed, how her ears popped, and then the roar—a sound she had never heard before and could not forget. She had held onto a steel beam, certain she was going to die, and had screamed for help that did not come until dawn.

In the months that followed, Sofia did not talk about it. She returned to duty, went through the motions, and told herself she was fine. But she was not fine. The first time it rained hard—a summer thunderstorm that rolled in fast—she found herself standing in the middle of her kitchen, heart pounding, unable to remember walking there. Her husband, Marco, asked if she was okay, and she snapped at him for no reason she could explain. What frightened her most was the feeling that she was not really there, that she had become something hollow. She had come to believe that her reactions since the storm proved she was a lousy coper, that other people would have handled it better, that something inside her had broken and could not be fixed. She felt like an object, not like a person, going through the motions of her life without actually living it.

The triggers multiplied. Any weather that reminded her of that night—the same heavy humidity, the same gray-green sky, the same pressure drop before a storm—would send her into a state of hypervigilance that she could not control. She began scanning her surroundings constantly, checking for escape routes every time she walked into a room, whether it was the mess hall, the PX, or her own living room. Loud noises were the worst. A truck backfiring in the motor pool would make her jump so violently that her commanding officer noticed and asked if she was getting enough sleep. She started to avoid being outside when the sky looked uncertain, and she began to dread the sound of wind. Even the presence of a police car on the road made her chest tighten, though she could not say why—it was authority, she supposed, the feeling of being helpless and waiting for someone to save her.

The causal connections tightened into a loop she could not escape. Each time a trigger appeared—the rumble of thunder, the crack of a door slamming—it activated her threat system, and she would startle, scan, plan escape routes. But the threat itself then reinforced her negative appraisals: see how jumpy I am, see how scared, I really am a lousy coper. And those appraisals, in turn, made her more sensitive to triggers. She began to believe that she could not stop bad things from happening to her, that the world was fundamentally unsafe, and that belief made her scan for danger even more. She would find herself checking the weather forecast obsessively, and then feel ashamed for doing so. The more she felt like an object, the more she avoided situations where she might feel exposed—she stopped going to the gym on base because the echo of weights dropping sounded too much like debris hitting metal.

At work, her performance did not suffer visibly, but she had stopped volunteering for field exercises. She found reasons to stay in the office, to keep her back to a wall, to keep the door open. Marco had started sleeping in the guest room because she would wake up gasping, and she could not explain to him what she was afraid of. What finally brought her to the clinic was a drill. A simulated explosion during a training exercise—a controlled blast, she knew it was controlled—sent her into a full panic. She locked herself in a supply closet and could not come out until a fellow soldier found her twenty minutes later, shaking and crying. She was certain she would be discharged, that her career was over, that everyone would see her for what she really was. But what frightened her most, sitting in the waiting room, was the thought that nothing would change. She was hoping, barely, that someone could tell her how to stop feeling like a ghost in her own body.
